title: Exchange Rates
in30Seconds: An exchange rate is the price of one currency measured in another: how many dollars a euro costs, or how many yen a dollar buys. The same rate can be written two ways, and the two are reciprocals. When a currency buys more foreign money it has appreciated; when it buys less it has depreciated. In a floating system supply and demand set the rate, and a weaker home currency makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home.
whyItMatters: Exchange rates connect a national economy to the rest of the world. They decide what an imported car, a foreign vacation, or a barrel of oil costs in your own currency, and whether a country's exporters can win foreign customers. Firms that buy or sell across borders live and die by these numbers, and hedging currency risk is a core finance skill. For a citizen, the exchange rate quietly shapes prices at the store and the competitiveness of local jobs. Understanding how quotes are read and what moves them is the entry point to international finance, trade, and monetary policy.
learningObjectives: Define an exchange rate and explain why a single rate can be quoted two reciprocal ways.
Convert an amount between two currencies given a quoted rate.
Distinguish appreciation from depreciation and identify which currency strengthened.
Explain what moves a floating exchange rate: relative interest rates, relative inflation, trade flows, and expectations.
Analyze how a stronger or weaker home currency changes the cost of exports and imports.
Distinguish floating from fixed/pegged exchange-rate regimes and state the core tradeoff.

collegeVersion.heading: What an exchange rate is, and how to read a quote
collegeVersion.body: An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in units of another. Like any price, it is a ratio, so it can be written two ways that carry exactly the same information. If one euro costs 1.10 U.S. dollars, then one U.S. dollar costs 1 / 1.10 = about 0.91 euros. These two numbers are reciprocals: quoting 'dollars per euro' and 'euros per dollar' are just two views of the same market. This is the single most common source of confusion for beginners, because whether a rising number means the home currency is getting stronger or weaker depends entirely on which way the quote is written. The reliable habit is to name the units out loud. If the quote is dollars per euro and it rises from 1.10 to 1.20, each euro now costs more dollars, so the euro has strengthened and the dollar has weakened. Because the two currencies sit on opposite sides of one ratio, whenever one appreciates the other must depreciate by a matching proportion.

collegeVersion.heading: Appreciation and depreciation
collegeVersion.body: A currency appreciates, or strengthens, when its exchange rate rises so that it buys more of another currency. It depreciates, or weakens, when it buys less. These are relative statements: a currency never strengthens in the abstract, only against some other currency over some period. The words 'strong' and 'weak' are descriptions, not value judgments. A strong currency is pleasant for travelers and importers, who get more foreign goods per unit of home money, but hard on exporters, whose goods now look expensive abroad. A weak currency is the mirror image. Under a fixed exchange-rate regime the deliberate policy versions of these moves have their own names: a government devalues when it officially lowers its pegged rate and revalues when it raises it, whereas appreciation and depreciation describe market-driven moves under floating.

collegeVersion.heading: What determines a floating exchange rate
collegeVersion.body: In a floating system the rate is set by supply and demand for the currency in the foreign exchange market, the largest financial market in the world. Demand for a currency comes from everyone who needs it: importers buying its country's goods, tourists visiting, foreign firms making direct investments, and portfolio investors buying its bonds and stocks. Four forces move that supply and demand. First, relative interest rates and expected returns: when a country's assets pay more than others, capital flows in to buy them, raising demand for the currency and pushing it up. Second, relative inflation: a currency losing purchasing power to fast domestic inflation tends to depreciate, and over long horizons rates drift toward purchasing power parity, the level that would equalize the price of the same goods across countries. Third, trade flows: a country selling more exports than it imports generates foreign demand for its currency. Fourth, expectations: because traders act on where they think the rate is headed, a belief that a currency will rise increases demand and cuts supply today, which can make moves self-reinforcing and volatile in the short run. Interest rates are the strongest short-run lever, which is why exchange rates react sharply to central-bank news; how those rates get set belongs to the monetary-policy topic.

collegeVersion.heading: How currency strength affects exports and imports
collegeVersion.body: Exchange-rate movements change incentives to trade. A weaker home currency makes that country's exports cheaper for foreign buyers, because their own money now converts into more of it, and simultaneously makes imports more expensive at home. A stronger home currency does the reverse: exports look dear abroad while imports become cheap. This is why a large currency swing ripples through an economy, shifting aggregate demand as net exports rise or fall. It is tempting to conclude that a weak currency is simply 'good' because it boosts exports, but that overlooks the cost: imports and foreign travel become more expensive, and inputs that firms buy from abroad cost more. Exchange rates tie the two sides together, which is why economists resist labeling exports 'good' and imports 'bad.'

collegeVersion.heading: Floating versus fixed regimes
collegeVersion.body: Countries choose how much to let the market set their rate, along a spectrum. At one end, a pure float lets supply and demand determine the rate with no official target; the U.S. dollar floats, and neither the U.S. Treasury nor the Federal Reserve targets a level for it. A soft peg or managed float lets the market lead but has the central bank intervene, buying or selling its own currency, to smooth moves it considers excessive. A hard peg fixes the rate and defends it with foreign-exchange reserves and monetary policy. At the far end, a country can abandon its own currency and adopt another's, as Ecuador did with the dollar. The central tradeoff runs through all of these: a fixed rate delivers certainty that lowers currency risk and can encourage trade, but it forces domestic monetary policy to serve the peg rather than fight a local recession or inflation. A float keeps that policy freedom but accepts a rate that can swing substantially and unpredictably. Economists genuinely disagree about which is better; the right answer depends on a country's circumstances rather than on a universal rule.

vocabulary.definition: The price of one currency stated in units of another, such as 1.10 U.S. dollars for one euro.
The same exchange rate written the other way around; dollars-per-euro and euros-per-dollar are each one divided into the other.
A rise in a currency's value so that it buys more of another currency; the currency has strengthened.
A fall in a currency's value so that it buys less of another currency; the currency has weakened.
A rate set by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market, with no official target level.
A rate a government or central bank sets and defends at a chosen value using reserves and policy.
A deliberate official lowering of a fixed exchange rate by the authority that sets the peg (revaluation is the opposite).
The long-run idea that exchange rates tend toward the level that would make identical goods cost the same across countries.
The global market where currencies are traded and their relative prices are determined.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Money from another country is a thing you can buy, and the exchange rate is its price tag. If a euro costs 1.10 dollars, then a dollar costs about 0.91 euros, which is just the same price flipped over. When a currency gets more expensive to buy, we say it got stronger; when it gets cheaper, it got weaker. A weaker dollar is like your country putting everything it sells on sale for foreigners, because their money now buys more of ours, while the foreign things we want to buy cost us more.
eli10.analogy: Think of currencies like tokens at two different arcades. The exchange rate is how many of your tokens the counter gives you for a friend's tokens. If the rate moves so your token fetches more of theirs, your token got stronger; if it fetches fewer, it got weaker. And the counter's two signs, 'yours for theirs' and 'theirs for yours,' are the same deal read from opposite ends.
eli10.analogyLimits: The arcade counter usually has one fixed posted rate, but real exchange rates float and change second by second as millions of traders buy and sell. Arcade tokens also have no interest rate or inflation behind them, so the analogy captures how to read a quote but not what makes a real rate rise or fall.

workedExample: Suppose the quoted rate is 1.10 dollars per euro (an illustrative rate, not a current market figure). A U.S. traveler faces a 200-euro hotel bill, so it costs 200 x 1.10 = 220 dollars. Written the other way, one dollar buys 1 / 1.10 = 0.91 euros. Now the dollar weakens and the rate moves to 1.20 dollars per euro, meaning the euro has appreciated about 9%. The same 200-euro bill now costs 200 x 1.20 = 240 dollars: the import got dearer for the American, exactly what a weaker home currency does. The flip side helps U.S. sellers. A U.S. export priced at 1,000 dollars cost a European buyer 1,000 / 1.10 = 909 euros before, but only 1,000 / 1.20 = 833 euros after the dollar weakened, so it is now cheaper abroad and easier to sell.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a rising exchange-rate number as always meaning the home currency got stronger.
commonMistakes.correction: It depends on which way the quote is written. If the quote is dollars-per-euro, a rising number means the euro strengthened and the dollar weakened. Always name the units before deciding.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking a strong currency is always good and a weak one always bad.
commonMistakes.correction: A strong currency helps importers and travelers but hurts exporters; a weak one helps exporters but raises import prices. Each has winners and losers, so 'strong' and 'weak' are not grades.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing a weaker currency makes exports more expensive abroad.
commonMistakes.correction: It is the opposite. A weaker home currency means foreigners' money converts into more of it, so home-country exports become cheaper for them, while imports become more expensive at home.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming exchange rates always float freely, set only by markets.
commonMistakes.correction: Regimes range from free floats to managed floats, soft and hard pegs, and full adoption of another currency. Under a peg the government defends a chosen value with reserves and policy.
Depreciation is a market-driven fall under floating; devaluation is a deliberate official lowering of a pegged rate by the authority that sets it.

compareContrast.distinction: Appreciation is a currency rising so it buys more foreign money (it strengthened); depreciation is it falling so it buys less (it weakened). Because a rate is a ratio, one currency's appreciation is the other's depreciation.

A floating rate is set by market supply and demand with no target and keeps monetary policy free; a fixed rate is set and defended by the central bank using reserves, buying certainty at the cost of policy independence.
A weaker home currency makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home; a stronger home currency makes imports cheaper and exports look expensive to foreign buyers.

keyTakeaway: An exchange rate is just the price of one currency in another, readable two reciprocal ways; in a floating system supply and demand (driven by interest rates, inflation, trade, and expectations) set it, and a weaker home currency cheapens exports while making imports more expensive.

questionBank.prompt: An exchange rate is best defined as:
options: The price of one currency expressed in units of another currency
The total quantity of foreign currency a country holds in reserve
The interest rate a central bank charges banks that borrow from it
The percentage by which prices rise across an economy in a year
questionBank.explanation: An exchange rate is a price: how much of one currency it takes to buy a unit of another. Option B describes foreign-exchange reserves, a stock a central bank holds, not the rate. Option C is the policy or discount interest rate. Option D is the inflation rate. Only A states what an exchange rate measures.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the definition of an exchange rate

questionBank.prompt: The quote for the euro against the dollar moves from 1.10 dollars per euro to 1.20 dollars per euro. Which statement is correct?
options: The dollar appreciated and the euro depreciated
Both currencies appreciated at the same time
The euro appreciated and the dollar depreciated
Neither currency changed value; only the quote's format changed
questionBank.explanation: Each euro now costs more dollars, so the euro buys more dollars than before: the euro appreciated and, because a rate is one ratio, the dollar depreciated. A is backwards. B is impossible, since one currency's appreciation against another is the other's depreciation. D is wrong because the numbers, not just the format, changed.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing appreciation from depreciation by reading a quote

questionBank.prompt: If one U.S. dollar buys 0.80 British pounds, how many dollars does it take to buy an item priced at 40 pounds?
options: 32 dollars
50 dollars
40 dollars
0.02 dollars
questionBank.explanation: At 0.80 pounds per dollar, one pound costs 1 / 0.80 = 1.25 dollars, so 40 pounds cost 40 x 1.25 = 50 dollars. Option A (32) wrongly multiplies 40 x 0.80, applying the rate in the wrong direction. Option C ignores the rate. Option D divides incorrectly. The key is to convert using the reciprocal that gives dollars per pound.
questionBank.skill: Converting an amount between currencies using a quoted rate

questionBank.prompt: A country's currency depreciates sharply against its trading partners. All else equal, the most likely effect is that:
options: Its exports become more expensive abroad and its imports become cheaper at home
Both its exports and its imports become cheaper for everyone involved
Its exports and imports are unaffected because trade depends only on tariffs
Its exports become cheaper abroad and its imports become more expensive at home
questionBank.explanation: A weaker currency means foreigners' money converts into more of it, so the country's exports get cheaper for them, while home buyers need more of their weakened currency to afford imports, making imports dearer. A reverses both effects. B is impossible, since a currency move helps one side of trade and hurts the other. C wrongly claims exchange rates do not matter for trade.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing how currency strength affects exports and imports

questionBank.prompt: In a floating exchange-rate system, which change would most directly tend to make a country's currency appreciate?
options: A surge in domestic inflation well above its trading partners' inflation
A government announcement abandoning any target for the currency
A rise in the country's interest rates that pulls in foreign investment
A central bank fixing the rate below its current market level
questionBank.explanation: Higher relative interest rates raise the return on the country's assets, attracting foreign capital that must buy the currency, which raises demand and appreciates it. A pushes the other way: high relative inflation erodes purchasing power and tends to depreciate a currency. B describes floating itself, not a directional force. D is an intervention that would hold the rate down, not let it appreciate.
questionBank.skill: Identifying determinants that move a floating exchange rate
